insight.step: Introduce two people you know who have never met but would get along.

options.label: A few close people around a long table

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you value conversations that can go somewhere. People like you tend to judge an evening by whether one real thing got said, not by how loud it was, and are likely to be the one who lingers at the table long after dessert.
insight.step: Invite two people for a simple meal this month, even if it isn't a special day.

options.label: Just one person who really knows me

insight.reveal: Your answer points to someone who finds big celebrations of themselves a little uncomfortable. Being truly seen by one person matters more to you than being cheered by many, and you tend to prefer deep talks over small talk on ordinary days too.
insight.step: Tell the person you thought of what they mean to you, before your next birthday comes.

options.label: Alone, with something great to eat

insight.reveal: This answer reflects a feeling that attention on your day can be more pressure than gift. People like you tend to enjoy their own company and treat themselves well, and often give generously on others' birthdays while quietly hoping their own passes softly.
insight.step: Treat yourself to one great meal alone this week, and let it be enough.

questions.prompt: You win a huge amount of money tomorrow. What do you do first?

options.label: Call my family and share the news

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that good news only feels complete for you once it is shared. People with this orientation tend to celebrate colleagues' wins loudly, remember everyone's birthdays, and often find a quiet solo triumph oddly flat until they have told someone close.
insight.research: Spending money on other people lifted people's happiness more than spending the same money on themselves.
insight.step: Share one small piece of good news with someone today, even if it feels too small.

options.label: Stay calm, make a plan, change little

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you trust slow, steady thinking over the rush of a big moment. People like you tend to read the small print before signing anything, keep the routines that already work, and are often the calm person others phone first when a crisis lands.
insight.step: Write down three things in your life you would keep exactly the same, whatever happened.

options.label: Quit my job that same week

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a life where time matters more than money. People with this orientation often already know exactly which part of their week they would cut first, tend to act fast once a door opens, and bring real energy to fresh starts that others would plan to death.
insight.step: Name the one part of your work week you would drop first, and find one small way to shrink it.

options.label: Tell no one, afraid of how people would change

insight.reveal: This answer reflects a deep wish to be valued for who you are, not for what you have. People who think this way tend to watch closely who stays near when things change, keep good news to a small circle, and are often the most loyal friend once trust is earned.
insight.step: Notice this week who in your life you'd trust with big news. That list is worth knowing.

questions.prompt: Do brand names on clothes and bags matter to you?

options.label: Not at all. I want comfort

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that you judge things by how they feel, not by what they say about you. People like you tend to wear favourite clothes until they fall apart, read status in other ways, like who gets listened to, and are often more impressed by how someone treats a waiter than by their bag.
insight.step: This week, notice one sign of status you do care about that has nothing to do with things.

options.label: Quality yes, logos no

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you like luxury you can feel but others can't see. People with this orientation tend to compare purchases carefully, buy fewer things that last for years, and often quietly enjoy being underestimated by people who only read loud signals.
insight.step: Use one 'good' item you're saving this week, on an ordinary day.

options.label: A little. I notice what others wear

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a sharp eye for the small signals people send. You are likely to read rooms quickly, remember what someone wore to a party months ago and spot a new haircut first, though on less sure days the same eye can drift into quiet comparing.
insight.step: Next time you notice what someone wears, also notice one thing about them that cost nothing.

options.label: Yes. I feel more respected in them

insight.reveal: This answer reflects how clothes can work like armour for you, a way to walk into a room already accepted. People with this orientation often had to earn respect early, tend to take great care with how they present themselves, and are often the friend others ask for help before a big interview.
insight.step: Wear your plainest outfit to one ordinary event this week and notice how people actually treat you.

questions.prompt: A close friend suddenly becomes rich. Your honest first feeling?

options.label: Pure happiness for them

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that you keep your scoreboard switched off with the people you love. People like you tend to be the first to raise a glass at a friend's promotion, celebrate without a trace of edge, and are often the person others call first with good news, knowing your joy will be real.
insight.step: Congratulate someone this week on a win, and ask them what part of it they're proudest of.

options.label: Curious how they did it

insight.reveal: Picking this suggests you turn other people's luck into a puzzle worth solving. People with this orientation tend to learn faster from friends than from books, ask the questions others feel too polite to ask, and often leave a dinner with a new idea for their own life.
insight.step: Ask someone you admire this week one specific question about how they got where they are.

options.label: A small sting of envy

insight.reveal: Your answer points to unusual honesty about your own feelings, not a lack of kindness. People who admit the sting tend to be candid friends who tell you the truth about a haircut, and their envy often works like a compass, pointing straight at what they want for themselves.
insight.step: Next time you feel envy, finish the sentence 'I wish I had…' in your head. That's the real goal.

options.label: Worry they'll leave me behind

insight.reveal: This answer reflects how friendships can feel fragile to you when the balance between people shifts. People with this orientation tend to stay loyal for years, quietly track who reached out last, and often worry that their care is not returned in equal measure.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety, a worry about rejection, and it shapes how relationships feel.
insight.step: Reach out to a friend whose life has changed recently, without mentioning the change.

questions.prompt: Which life pulls at you more?

options.label: A small home, lots of free time

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that you measure wealth in hours rather than things. People like you tend to feel richest on a slow morning with nothing booked, turn down promotions that eat their evenings, and are often surprisingly content on a budget others would find tight.
insight.step: Give yourself one slow morning this week with nothing scheduled before ten.

options.label: Comfort, plus a few real luxuries

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you know exactly which luxuries are worth it to you and which are just noise. People with this orientation tend to spend big on one thing, like a good bed, great coffee or a yearly trip, and almost nothing elsewhere, which often makes their money stretch further.
insight.step: Name your one 'worth it' luxury and enjoy it slowly this week, without rushing.

options.label: Big success, whatever it takes

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a drive for proof more than possessions: proof you were right, or that you could. People like you tend to thrive on bold targets and visible scoreboards, rally teams around a big goal, and often find the drive started long before money was the reason.
insight.step: Write down who you'd most want to see your success. Then ask yourself why them.

options.label: I want simple, but I keep chasing more

insight.reveal: This answer reflects two pulls living in you at once. People who feel this tend to hold a clear picture of 'enough' while fearing that stopping early means losing, so they may browse cottage listings on the way to a job they keep pushing harder at. Seeing that gap clearly is a real strength.
insight.step: Picture a normal week in your 'enough' life. Find one piece of it you could have this month.

questions.prompt: Dinner with friends who earn more than you. The bill comes. You…

options.label: Split it evenly, no fuss

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that you value the mood of an evening over the exact numbers. People like you tend to remember who was fun rather than who ordered the expensive bottle, keep group plans easy, and are often the friend everyone wants at the table.
insight.step: Next time you eat out, suggest one place that you choose, and see how it feels to lead.

options.label: Quietly do the math in my head

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you carry a quiet calculator into social life. People with this orientation tend to be scrupulously fair, often know their monthly spending almost to the coin, and may feel a tension others don't notice, yet say nothing to keep the peace.
insight.step: Next time it feels uneven, say so lightly once and watch how little drama it causes.

options.label: Order less so I don't overspend

insight.reveal: Your answer points to someone who protects friendships by quietly adjusting themselves. People like you tend to be modest with money and generous with attention, though the same habit can show up elsewhere as taking the smaller seat, the worse room or the last turn.
insight.step: At your next meal out, order the thing you actually want, just once.

options.label: Act fine, then stress about it later

insight.reveal: This answer reflects that you would rather pay with worry than risk an awkward moment. People with this orientation are often the most generous in the group, tend to replay the evening on the way home, and rarely let anyone see what it cost them.
insight.step: Suggest a cheaper plan to one friend this week, like a walk or cooking together.

questions.prompt: You walk into a very fancy hotel lobby. How do you feel?

options.label: At ease. I enjoy places like this

insight.reveal: Your response indicates a natural ease in polished spaces. People like you tend to feel comfortable in most rooms, chat easily with concierges and strangers, and often help nervous friends relax, which makes the rare places where you do feel out of step worth noticing.
insight.step: Go somewhere this week where you're a beginner, and notice how you carry yourself.

options.label: Excited, like it's a special treat

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you still feel genuine wonder at nice things, which many people lose. People with this orientation tend to get more joy from one rare treat than others get from daily luxury, photograph the hotel breakfast, and often make ordinary outings feel like an occasion for everyone.
insight.step: Plan one small special treat for later this week, and enjoy the waiting as much as the treat.

options.label: A bit bored. It's all for show

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a sharp eye for anything performed. People like you tend to prefer the small family-run place over the grand chain and spot marketing tricks instantly, though the same eye can make it hard to enjoy a compliment without quietly checking if it's real.
insight.step: Accept the next compliment you get with just 'thank you', no checking, no deflecting.

options.label: Like someone will notice I don't belong

insight.reveal: This answer reflects a quiet inner voice that checks whether you are allowed to be somewhere. People who hear it tend to feel it in meetings and new groups too, even when welcome, and are often the most considerate guests in any room because they notice who else feels left out.
insight.research: Friends often judge traits like intelligence and creativity more accurately than we judge ourselves.
insight.step: Ask a friend which room they think you belong in most. Their answer may surprise you.

questions.prompt: You meet someone wearing a very expensive watch. First thought?

options.label: Nice watch. That's it

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that you give people a clean first impression. People like you tend to judge others by what they do next rather than what they wear, are slower than most to decide who someone is, and often end up with an unusually varied circle of friends.
insight.step: Next time you meet someone new, guess one thing about them, then check it later.

options.label: I wonder what they do for work

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests your mind turns objects into stories about paths and choices. People with this orientation tend to ask strangers about their careers, enjoy biographies and job stories, and often quietly map other people's lives against their own.
insight.step: Ask one person this week how they ended up in their job, and listen for the turning point.

options.label: They're trying to impress someone

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a strong respect for humility and a quick eye for performance. People like you tend to be trusted at work because they play it straight, often downplay their own wins, and may hesitate to enjoy nice things without a flicker of suspicion.
insight.research: A trait called Honesty-Humility predicts integrity and rule-breaking at work better than the classic five personality traits alone.
insight.step: Mention one thing you're proud of to someone this week, plainly, without a joke.

options.label: I quietly compare myself and come up short

insight.reveal: This answer reflects how other people's things can feel like a score you're being measured against. People with this orientation tend to be ambitious and highly alert to detail, though they often compare on many fronts and rarely count the things they have that others would want.
insight.step: Write down three things someone might envy about your life, then read them once a day this week.

questions.prompt: Growing up, how did money feel in your home?

options.label: Rarely talked about. It was just there

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that money sat quietly in the background of your early life. People like you tend to stay calm about bills and take financial surprises in stride, yet often know less about their friends' money lives than their love lives, because money talk can feel oddly awkward.
insight.step: Ask someone you trust one simple money question this week, like what they enjoy spending on.

options.label: Tight, but we managed

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you learned early how to make a little go a long way. People with this orientation tend to check prices out of habit even when they don't need to, are brilliant at stretching a budget, and often find spending generously on themselves feels strangely like breaking a rule.
insight.step: Buy yourself one small thing this week without checking the price first.

options.label: Money caused arguments

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a home where money carried tension. People who grew up this way tend to feel their body tighten when money comes up and may avoid money talk with a partner to protect the peace, yet they often become unusually skilled at keeping finances calm and open as adults.
insight.step: Start one calm, short money chat this week with someone close, at a relaxed moment.

options.label: Something I still feel uneasy about today

insight.reveal: This answer reflects how the money feelings of childhood can still live in your adult days. People who notice this tend to find their unease doesn't track their bank balance, a sign it is about safety more than numbers, and that kind of self-awareness is often the first step to feeling settled.
insight.step: Next time money worry rises, ask: 'Is this about today, or about back then?' and just notice the answer.

questions.prompt: You get some unexpected extra money this month. Where does it go?

options.label: Put aside for later

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that security feels better to you than a quick thrill. People like you tend to build a cushion before friends have even made a plan, stay steady during money scares, and often delay small joys long after they could easily afford them.
insight.step: Do one small thing this week you've been 'saving up' to enjoy, even a tiny one.

options.label: A meal or trip with people I love

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you turn money into memories with people in them. People with this orientation tend to organise the group trip, remember shared meals in detail years later, and often find those choices grow in value because the story gets retold every time you meet.
insight.research: People often report that experiences they paid for made them happier than possessions they bought.
insight.step: Suggest a simple shared plan with someone this week, like a picnic or a cheap dinner.

options.label: Something just for me

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a healthy instinct to enjoy good fortune while it is fresh. People like you tend to put others first for most of the year, so a treat for yourself is often one of the few moments you act as if your own wants count as much as everyone else's.
insight.step: Notice one want of your own this week and say it out loud to someone.

options.label: It's gone before I even notice

insight.reveal: This answer reflects how money slips easily into the flow of your small daily wants. People with this orientation tend to be spontaneous and generous with coffees and last-minute plans, and often find that later feels very far away from now, which can make saving feel abstract.
insight.research: People with stronger present bias, preferring smaller rewards now over bigger ones later, are more likely to carry credit card debt.
insight.step: For three days, write down one small thing you spent on each evening, just to see the pattern.

questions.prompt: Your income doubles overnight. Would you be happier?

options.label: Yes, clearly

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that you know exactly which daily stresses more money would remove. People like you tend to be practical and clear-eyed about trade-offs, often keep a mental list of upgrades ready, and can usually tell which problems are about money and which ones aren't.
insight.research: For most people, happiness keeps rising with income; for the least happy group, it stops rising above a fairly high income.
insight.step: Name the one daily stress more money would fix, and find one free way to soften it this week.

options.label: A bit, then I'd get used to it

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you already know how fast new comforts become normal. People with this orientation tend to be hard to impress with things and easy to delight with surprises, and often prefer spending on new experiences that keep life feeling fresh.
insight.step: Surprise someone with a small unexpected gesture this week and notice your own mood after.

options.label: No. My real problems aren't about money

insight.reveal: Your answer points to one problem that no amount of money would touch: a relationship, a choice or a feeling. People like you tend to think deeply about what really matters, often know exactly which issue keeps them up at night, and are rarely fooled by quick fixes.
insight.research: For most people, happiness keeps rising with income; for the least happy group, it stops rising above a fairly high income.
insight.step: Spend ten quiet minutes this week on the problem money can't fix, just thinking it through.

options.label: I'd mostly worry about losing it

insight.reveal: This answer reflects a sense that, for you, having more simply means having more to lose. People with this orientation tend to be careful planners who check accounts often and insure what they own, and they often feel safest in the middle of things, where nothing can fall far.
insight.step: Next time you get something good, say 'this is good right now' before your mind jumps to losing it.

questions.prompt: If money and fear disappeared tomorrow, what would you do first?

options.label: Travel far, for a long time

insight.reveal: Your response indicates a hunger for distance as much as adventure. People like you tend to light up in unfamiliar cities and order the dish they can't pronounce, and often want a space where no one expects them to be who they usually are.
insight.step: Spend one afternoon this week somewhere in your area where no one knows you.

options.label: Start the thing I keep talking about

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests your dream is already specific, which puts you ahead of most. People with this orientation tend to keep notes, sketches or half-built plans in a drawer, and often wait for a perfect start date that keeps moving a little further away.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Write one when-then plan: 'When it's Saturday 10 a.m., I will spend 20 minutes on my idea.'

options.label: Honestly, I don't know what I'd want

insight.reveal: Your answer points to years spent being good at what was needed rather than what was wanted. People like you tend to be dependable at work and at home, and their own wishes often speak quietly. Not knowing is less an emptiness than a sign those wants deserve more room.
insight.step: Each evening this week, note one moment that made you feel more alive than usual.

options.label: Leave a job or relationship I've outgrown

insight.reveal: This answer reflects that you already know what you would change, and that fear, not clarity, is what's missing. People with this orientation tend to see their situation honestly, often rehearse the conversation in their head, and find that naming it, even silently, is the first real step.
insight.step: Write down one small thing you could change about that situation this month, without leaving it.

questions.prompt: Which kind of regret visits you most often?

options.label: Something I said

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that you care deeply about how your words land. People like you tend to replay conversations in the shower, are often the first to apologise, and can be the last to accept an apology for themselves.
insight.step: Next time a sentence replays in your head, ask the person directly if it bothered them.

options.label: A chance I didn't take

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests the roads you didn't take still feel open in your mind. People with this orientation tend to regret inaction more than mistakes, which often makes them braver than they think when the next chance appears.
insight.step: Say yes to one small invitation this week that you'd normally talk yourself out of.

options.label: Someone I lost touch with

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a heart that keeps old friendships alive long after contact fades. People like you tend to remember the birthdays of friends they haven't seen in years, and often assume the other person moved on, when they may be waiting for the same first message you hesitate to send.
insight.step: Send that person one short message this week. No need to explain the gap.

options.label: Years spent being who others wanted

insight.reveal: This answer reflects a clear view of the gap between who you were and who you showed. People who notice this tend to be deeply tuned in to others, and have often already started closing that gap, choosing honesty in small moments that once would have slipped by.
insight.step: Make one small choice this week purely because you want it, not because it pleases anyone.

questions.prompt: Two offers: a safe job, or a risky one doing what you love. You…

options.label: Take the safe job

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that you value stability as a foundation for everything else. People like you tend to feed their passions on the side, where no boss can take them away, and often protect what they love by keeping it out of anyone else's hands.
insight.step: Give one hour this week to the thing you love, with no plan to turn it into money.

options.label: Ask for time and make long lists

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you trust lists more than your gut, even when your gut has quietly chosen already. People with this orientation tend to make thorough, careful decisions at work, and sometimes build long pros-and-cons lists to talk themselves out of what they already want.
insight.step: Next big choice, flip a coin. Notice which side you hoped for while it was in the air.

options.label: Take the risk, sort it out later

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a belief that you can handle almost any fall. People like you tend to change cities, careers or haircuts with little warning and adapt fast when plans collapse, though they sometimes leap to escape boredom rather than to reach a dream.
insight.step: Before your next leap, write one line on what you're running to, not just from.

options.label: Take the safe one and wonder forever

insight.reveal: This answer reflects that you know your heart and your fear well, and fear often wins the vote. People with this orientation tend to cheer loudly for friends' bold moves, and often take bigger risks for others than they let themselves take.
insight.step: Take one tiny risk for yourself this week, something you'd easily encourage a friend to do.

questions.prompt: Who knows about your biggest dream?

options.label: Everyone. I talk about it a lot

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that you use other people as a promise you can't easily break. People like you tend to recruit cheerleaders and spark energy in a group, though sometimes the talking feels so good it quietly replaces the doing.
insight.step: This week, take one step toward your dream before telling anyone about it.

options.label: One or two close people

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you guard your dream like something fragile. People with this orientation tend to pick their audience carefully, choosing the few who will believe in it without asking for proof, and are often fiercely supportive of other people's dreams in return.
insight.step: Update one of those people on your dream this week, even if there's little progress.

options.label: No one. Saying it would make it real

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a fear of the look on someone's face more than of failure itself. People like you tend to work quietly and reveal things only when they are finished, which can be impressive, though a dream that is not spoken also can't be helped.
insight.step: Tell one kind person a small part of your dream this week, just one sentence.

options.label: I've stopped admitting it even to myself

insight.reveal: This answer reflects a dream that went quiet to protect you from wanting it. People who say this often still feel it in odd moments: a song, a film, or someone else's success that stings more than it should. That sting is useful, because it shows the wish is still alive.
insight.step: Notice the next time someone else's success stings. Ask what it reminds you of.

questions.prompt: Someone your age achieves exactly your dream. You feel…

options.label: Inspired. It's possible!

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that you see the world as having room for everyone. People like you tend to be good friends to ambitious people, who often feel judged elsewhere, and often turn someone else's success into a practical map for their own next move.
insight.step: Look up how that person started, and find one step they took that you could take too.

options.label: Fired up to catch up

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests a rival is better fuel for you than a goal. People with this orientation tend to do their best work when someone is just ahead, keep an eye on the leaderboard at the gym, and often drift a little when they are alone out in front.
insight.step: Choose a friendly 'rival' this week and share one small goal with them.

options.label: Quietly crushed for a day or two

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a private timeline in your head for where you should be by now. People like you tend to hold high standards and feel things deeply, so the pain is often less about the other person and more about that inner clock, which can be gently reset.
insight.step: Write down where you thought you'd be by now. Then cross out the date and keep the goal.

options.label: Relief. Now I don't have to try

insight.reveal: This answer reflects a dream that carried a weight of pressure along with the hope. People who feel relief here often discover the dream was partly someone else's, and tend to find that letting it go frees up energy for a goal that is truly yours.
insight.step: Ask yourself this week: which of my goals did I choose, and which did I inherit?

questions.prompt: It's Sunday night. What's mostly on your mind?

options.label: Plans for the week ahead

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that you feel calm once the week has a shape. People like you tend to prep meals, check calendars and lay out clothes on Sunday, rarely miss deadlines, and often find surprise weekends more stressful than fun.
insight.step: Leave one evening this week totally unplanned and see what you choose to do with it.

options.label: Not much. I'm relaxed

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you have work that fits your life well, or a strong wall between the two. People with this orientation tend to sleep easily and bounce back quickly from bad days, which is something many people spend years trying to build.
insight.step: Notice what keeps your Sunday calm, and protect that one habit this week.

options.label: A quiet 'is this it?'

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a feeling of being unfinished rather than unhappy. People like you tend to crave growth and fresh challenges, and the question often returns at the same time each week, a clue that it may be about routine more than your whole life.
insight.step: Add one new thing to next Sunday evening, even a small one, and see if the feeling changes.

options.label: The life I'd live if I were braver

insight.reveal: This answer reflects a clear second life you can see next to your current one. People who carry this picture tend to be vivid imaginers who often already know its first step, and keep it waiting for the right Monday.
insight.step: This Monday, do one five-minute action from that braver life.

questions.prompt: When you set a big goal, what usually happens?

options.label: I make a plan and stick to it

insight.reveal: Your response indicates strong follow-through once you have committed. People like you tend to finish courses, hit savings targets and keep streaks going, and often find goals easy and rest hard, which can make it tricky to drop a goal that no longer fits.
insight.research: Personality traits predict life outcomes such as health, divorce and career success about as well as family income and intelligence do.
insight.step: Look at one current goal this week and ask: do I still want this, or just want to finish it?

options.label: Start strong, fade by week three

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you run on excitement, and excitement often runs out before a habit forms. People with this orientation tend to be brilliant starters who bring real energy to new projects, and often succeed best when the goal is tiny and the first step is easy.
insight.research: In one study, new daily habits took a median of 66 days to become automatic, and missing a single day did not ruin progress.
insight.step: Pick a goal you dropped and restart it at a size so small it feels silly.

options.label: I keep it vague so I can't fail

insight.reveal: Your answer points to someone who cares a lot about getting things right. People like you tend to keep goals loose so no one, including you, can say you missed, which feels safe but also means no one can say you made it. A small, named target often unlocks a lot.
insight.research: Across 94 studies, making a specific when-then plan had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals.
insight.step: Turn one vague goal into a when-then plan: 'When X happens, I will do Y.'

options.label: I avoid setting goals. They stress me

insight.reveal: This answer reflects how goals can feel like a test you might fail. People with this orientation tend to grow more through curiosity than through targets, following whatever interests them, and often end up surprisingly far from where they started, in good ways.
insight.step: Instead of a goal, pick one question you're curious about and explore it for 20 minutes.

questions.prompt: Whose life do you secretly envy a little?

options.label: Someone who travels with no fixed home

insight.reveal: Your response indicates a wish for lightness as much as for travel. People like you tend to daydream about selling everything and love open-ended weekends, and the wish often points at whatever feels heavy in your life right now.
insight.step: Remove one small duty from your week that no one would really miss.

options.label: Someone who makes things for a living

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests part of you wants proof of your days, something you can hold. People with this orientation tend to feel restless in jobs where work disappears into emails and meetings, and often keep a creative side project that matters more than they admit.
insight.step: Make one small thing with your hands this week: a meal, a drawing, a repair.

options.label: An old friend who chose differently

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a road you once stood at too. People like you tend to keep quiet track of old classmates' lives, and the envy is often less about that person and more about a version of you who might have gone with them, which makes it a useful clue.
insight.step: Get in touch with that friend this month and ask what they miss about the road you took.

options.label: A version of me who made another choice

insight.reveal: This answer reflects a clear picture you keep of an alternate life. People who do this tend to be rich imaginers who often edit out that version's problems, and the most useful question is which piece of it you could still bring into the life you have.
insight.step: Name one quality of that 'other you' and try acting with it for one day this week.

questions.prompt: At 90, looking back, what would hurt most?

options.label: Places I never saw

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that you feel most alive when everything around you is new. People like you tend to plan the next trip before unpacking from the last and try new routes to work, and are likely to find that routine drains them faster than it drains others.
insight.step: Take a different route to somewhere you go every day, at least once this week.

options.label: Work I never finished or made

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you want to leave something behind with your name on it. People with this orientation tend to feel time pressure others don't, judge good days by what got built, and often keep working on a project long after others have gone home.
insight.step: Spend 25 minutes this week on the thing you'd most hate to leave unmade.

options.label: Love I didn't say out loud

insight.reveal: Your answer points to love that runs deep but often travels sideways, through help, jokes or simply showing up. People like you tend to fix a friend's shelf rather than say how much they matter, and often wait for a moment that doesn't quite feel right for the bigger words.
insight.research: People with stronger social relationships had about a 50% higher chance of survival over the study periods than people with weaker ones.
insight.step: Tell one person this week, in plain words, one thing you love about them.

options.label: Knowing I played it safe on purpose

insight.reveal: This answer reflects that you already feel the cost of caution while you're paying it. People who see this clearly tend to be thoughtful and self-aware, and are often closer to changing than people who don't ask the question at all.
insight.step: Do one thing this week that your 90-year-old self would be glad you did.

questions.prompt: When you really want something from someone, what do you do?

options.label: Ask for it directly

insight.reveal: Your response indicates a belief that a 'no' is just information, not a judgement. People like you tend to negotiate salaries and ask for what they need, and that ease can surprise others, who may need a little more warm-up than you do.
insight.step: Next time you ask for something, add one sentence about why it matters to you.

options.label: Drop hints and hope

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you want people to notice your wishes without you naming them, as proof they care. People with this orientation tend to be highly attentive to others' needs, but others rarely read hints as well as hinters hope, so the test is often failed unfairly.
insight.step: Turn one hint into a plain request this week: 'I'd love it if…'

options.label: Wait until someone offers

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a strong dislike of taking more than your share. People like you tend to be considerate guests and fair colleagues, though the cost can be quiet: good things often go to people who simply asked first.
insight.step: Ask for one small thing this week that you would normally wait to be offered.

options.label: Tell myself I didn't want it anyway

insight.reveal: This answer reflects a sense that, for you, not wanting feels safer than wanting and not getting. People with this orientation tend to seem easygoing and remarkably self-sufficient to others, while a private list of shrugged-off wishes quietly grows inside.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment avoidance, a discomfort with closeness, and it shapes how relationships feel.
insight.step: Catch one 'never mind' this week and say the real wish out loud instead.

questions.prompt: How do you most often show a partner affection?

options.label: Small touches during the day

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that affection lives in your hands as much as your words. People like you tend to reach for a partner's arm while walking, notice missing touch before anything else, and may feel a day without a hand on the shoulder as colder than a missed call.
insight.step: Next time your partner walks past, give them a light touch for no reason at all.

options.label: Saying it out loud, often

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests words feel like a promise to you, not decoration. People with this orientation tend to leave sweet notes and voice messages that make partners feel openly cherished, and may worry when a partner says it less, even when every other sign is there.
insight.step: This week, notice one way your partner shows love without words, and tell them you saw it.

options.label: I show it, but rarely say it

insight.reveal: Your answer points to love expressed through action: the fixed tap, the warmed-up car, the remembered favourite snack. People like you tend to give more than a partner realises, simply in a language they don't easily read, and may find the words themselves feel oddly heavy.
insight.step: Pair one thing you do for your partner this week with one sentence about why.

options.label: I wait for them to show it first

insight.reveal: This answer reflects how reaching out first can feel to you like a risk of not being met. People with this orientation tend to hold a lot of affection behind a door, waiting for proof it is safe, and once it is, they are often deeply devoted partners.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance, and both shape how relationships feel.
insight.step: Make the first warm move once this week, small and simple, and notice what comes back.

questions.prompt: What does a truly romantic evening look like to you?

options.label: Dinner somewhere new

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that newness itself feels romantic to you. People like you tend to feel attraction rise when they see a partner in an unfamiliar setting, enjoy the slight nerves of a new place, and are often the one who books the restaurant nobody has tried.
insight.step: Suggest one place neither of you has been for your next evening together.

options.label: Cooking together at home

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests romance for you lives inside teamwork. People with this orientation tend to feel most drawn to a partner while doing something side by side, like chopping onions or painting a room, rather than sitting face to face over candles.
insight.step: Cook one meal together this week with phones in another room.

options.label: A long talk with phones away

insight.reveal: Your answer points to desire that follows closeness, not the other way round. People like you tend to remember what a partner said far longer than what they wore, and being truly listened to may feel more intimate to you than any candlelit setting.
insight.step: Ask your partner one question tonight you've never asked them before.

options.label: Honestly, we've stopped planning these

insight.reveal: This answer reflects how romance may have slipped quietly behind your daily life. People who notice this are often the ones who miss it most, and that is a hopeful sign: the wish is still alive, and one small planned evening can often wake it back up.
insight.step: Plan one small evening for this week, even just a walk, and call it a date out loud.

questions.prompt: What usually draws you to someone first?

options.label: They make me laugh

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that you read humour as a sign of quick thinking and safety. People like you tend to flirt through teasing and in-jokes, and often lose interest fast when a partner stops being playful, even if everything else is fine.
insight.step: Start something playful with your partner or a friend this week, just to see who joins in.

options.label: Their confidence

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you're drawn to people who seem settled in themselves. People with this orientation often want someone steady enough that they can relax and stop holding everything together, and tend to bring plenty of their own spark to the pairing.
insight.step: Notice one moment this week when you felt fully at ease with someone. What made it so?

options.label: The way they look at me

insight.reveal: Your answer points to attraction that grows from being wanted. People like you tend to be warm, responsive partners who notice every glance, though desire can start as a mirror for you and fade quickly if that look of interest goes away.
insight.step: Look at your partner for a few seconds longer than usual this week, and see what changes.

options.label: Someone a little hard to read

insight.reveal: This answer reflects how uncertainty can feel exciting to you, sometimes more than comfort does. People with this orientation tend to feel intense, vivid chemistry, often mistake the rush of not knowing for a deeper match, and may find calm partners hard to fall for at first.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety, a worry about rejection, and it shapes how relationships feel.
insight.step: Next time someone feels 'too easy', give it one more conversation before deciding.

questions.prompt: When one of you leaves the house, what happens?

options.label: Always a kiss or hug goodbye

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that you protect closeness with small daily habits more than big gestures. People like you tend to keep rituals like a goodbye kiss or a goodnight text, build steady relationships, and notice right away when a goodbye is skipped.
insight.step: Make tomorrow's goodbye last five seconds longer than usual.

options.label: Sometimes, if we remember

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests affection is clearly there in your relationship but runs on autopilot. People with this orientation tend to be relaxed, easygoing partners who feel close in the big moments, and may drift a little in the ordinary days between them.
insight.step: Pick one daily moment, leaving or arriving, and make it a small ritual this week.

options.label: Rarely. We're deep in routine

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a relationship that feels comfortable more than close right now. Routine is a real sign of trust, and people like you tend to be dependable partners, though small touches are often the first thing to go and the easiest to bring back.
insight.step: Surprise your partner with a goodbye hug tomorrow, with no explanation.

options.label: I'd like to, but feel shy starting it

insight.reveal: This answer reflects how, even with someone close, reaching out can leave you feeling exposed. People who feel this tend to be tender and attentive, and often assume a partner doesn't want the hug, when that partner may be waiting too.
insight.step: Start one goodbye touch this week. Keep it small, and let it be enough.

questions.prompt: When do you feel the strongest desire for a partner?

options.label: After we've laughed together

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that you need to feel safe and light before you feel wanting. People like you tend to flirt through shared jokes and bring playfulness into the bedroom, and may find a stressful week dims desire more than they realise.
insight.step: Share something funny with your partner this week, on purpose, and notice the mood after.

options.label: Seeing them confident in their element

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests desire sparks when you see your partner as a separate person, not just part of 'us'. People with this orientation tend to feel a jolt watching a partner give a talk or fix something, and a bit of distance and admiration may do more for you than closeness alone.
insight.step: Watch your partner do something they're good at this week, and tell them what you noticed.

options.label: After some time apart

insight.reveal: Your answer points to needing space to miss someone before you can want them. People like you tend to love reunions after work trips and keep a healthy independent life, and may find constant closeness feels loving but not quite as exciting.
insight.step: Spend an evening apart this week doing your own thing, then notice how you feel on return.

options.label: Oddly, after we've had tension

insight.reveal: This answer reflects that closeness feels most urgent to you when it was briefly at risk. People with this orientation tend to feel relief and desire arrive together, which can make making up feel more intense than calm days, and they often care deeply about repair.
insight.step: This week, try creating that same closeness on a calm day, with an unexpected warm moment.

questions.prompt: In your relationship, who usually starts things in the bedroom?

options.label: Pretty equal, it goes both ways

insight.reveal: Your response indicates a relationship where you feel wanted without having to keep checking. People like you tend to share effort fairly in other areas too, like chores and plans, and the quiet risk is assuming the balance will stay without anyone talking about it.
insight.step: Tell your partner one thing you like about how they show they want you.

options.label: Mostly me

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you are confident and willing to go first. People with this orientation tend to make the plans and start the conversations, and often carry a hidden question: would anything happen if I stopped? A wish to be the one pursued sometimes is common here.
insight.step: Tell your partner, kindly and outside the bedroom, that you'd love them to start things sometimes.

options.label: Mostly my partner

insight.reveal: Your answer points to desire that arrives as a response rather than a spark. That is a common and normal pattern, and people like you tend to be warmly receptive, though a partner may read your waiting as less wanting than you actually feel.
insight.step: Make one small first move this week, even just a lingering kiss, and see how it lands.

options.label: Neither of us, lately

insight.reveal: This answer reflects a quiet standoff where you and your partner each wait for the other. People in this place often both miss intimacy and each believe the other has stopped wanting it, and simply naming the pause out loud tends to break it more easily than expected.
insight.research: In large samples, couples' well-being rose with how often they had sex up to about once a week, then levelled off.
insight.step: Start a gentle chat this week: 'I miss us being close. Do you?' Nothing more is needed.

questions.prompt: How do you honestly feel about how often you and a partner are intimate?

options.label: It feels about right

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that you judge intimacy by how close you feel, not by counting. People like you tend to trust the relationship enough not to keep score, roll with busy seasons, and often bring a calm that helps a partner relax too.
insight.research: In large samples, couples' well-being rose with how often they had sex up to about once a week, then levelled off.
insight.step: Tell your partner one recent moment of closeness you enjoyed, in or out of bed.

options.label: I'd like more

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests a deeper wish of yours: to feel chosen. People with this orientation tend to be openly affectionate and generous with attention, and may feel desire as reassurance, so a quiet week can feel like a message even when it isn't one.
insight.step: Ask your partner what helps them feel in the mood, and just listen to the answer.

options.label: I'd honestly like less

insight.reveal: Your answer points to an honest awareness of your own limits, which is a more common place to be than many admit. People who choose this often feel guilty about it, yet desire tends to respond to stress, sleep and feeling heard more than to the partner themselves.
insight.step: Notice this week which kinds of closeness you do want, and share one with your partner.

options.label: We never talk about it, so I'm not sure

insight.reveal: This answer reflects that intimacy in your relationship happens, or doesn't, in silence. Couples who skip this talk tend to each guess what the other wants, and often both guess wrong in the same careful direction, though the care behind that caution is a strength worth building on.
insight.step: Pick a relaxed moment this week and ask, lightly: 'Are you happy with how close we are?'

questions.prompt: Could you tell a partner plainly what you enjoy in bed?

options.label: Easily. We talk openly

insight.reveal: Your response indicates real ease with honest, intimate talk. People like you tend to find it easier to discuss other hard things too, like money, family and fears, and that openness may be the root of much of your relationship's strength.
insight.step: Ask your partner one open question this week about what they've been enjoying lately.

options.label: Only if they ask first

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you're open, but you need an invitation. People with this orientation tend to be generous, attentive partners who often assume a partner would ask if they wanted to know, while the partner assumes you'd say.
insight.step: Give the invitation yourself: ask your partner what they enjoy, and let them ask you back.

options.label: I hint or show instead of saying

insight.reveal: Your answer points to a striking twist: closeness comes easily to you, but naming it can feel like too much. People like you tend to communicate brilliantly through touch and timing, and often find words in this area more exposing than the act itself.
insight.step: Say one short, positive sentence this week about something you enjoyed together.

options.label: I've never really said it

insight.reveal: This answer reflects pleasure that has stayed private, even from people you trust. People who admit this tend to put a partner's comfort first and their own wants somewhere quiet, which shows real care, and a single honest sentence often opens more than they expect.
insight.step: Think of one thing you enjoy, and find a kind, simple way to tell your partner this week.

questions.prompt: A partner suggests trying something new together in bed. You feel…

options.label: Curious. Let's talk about it

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that you see intimacy as something a couple builds together, not a fixed routine. People like you tend to enjoy talking things through and asking good questions, and the conversation itself may be part of the excitement for you.
insight.step: Ask your partner one 'what if we…' question this week, about anything, and see where it goes.

options.label: Excited. I've wanted that too

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests you've been carrying wishes you hadn't voiced. People with this orientation tend to be adventurous and playful, often wait for a partner to open the door, then are surprised how easy walking through it turns out to be.
insight.step: Open the next door yourself: share one small new idea with your partner this week.

options.label: Nervous, but willing to talk

insight.reveal: Your answer points to someone who cares a lot about getting it right. People like you tend to value trust over novelty and take things at a comfortable pace, and with that trust in place, often find new things feel safe and even fun to try.
insight.step: Tell your partner what would help you feel at ease with something new. Only yes means yes.

options.label: Worried I'm not enough as I am

insight.reveal: This answer reflects how a new idea can sound like a review of you. People who feel this tend to be deeply invested in a partner's happiness, and often hear 'let's add' as 'you're missing', when most partners mean it as an invitation, not a complaint.
insight.research: Adults differ in attachment anxiety, a worry about rejection, and it shapes how relationships feel.
insight.step: Ask your partner directly: 'What do you love about us as we are?' and let the answer land.

questions.prompt: When do you feel most desirable?

options.label: After a day where I did well

insight.reveal: Your response indicates that being wanted and being capable are linked for you. People like you tend to feel most attractive after nailing a presentation or finishing a big task, and your confidence may rise and fall with your work week more than with your mirror.
insight.step: On your next good day, tell your partner about it, and notice whether closeness follows.

options.label: When I've made an effort to dress up

insight.reveal: Choosing this suggests confidence for you is something you can put on, like a key that unlocks a bolder self. People with this orientation tend to love any reason to dress for an occasion, and often enjoy being seen more than they'd ever say out loud.
insight.step: Dress up a little this week for no special reason, and see if your mood follows.

options.label: When my partner can't stop looking

insight.reveal: Your answer points to feeling desirable through another person's eyes more than your own. People like you tend to be wonderfully responsive to attention and warm in return, though it can feel cold on the days the looks don't come.
insight.step: Find one moment this week when you feel attractive alone, with no one watching.

options.label: Rarely. I wait to be told

insight.reveal: This answer reflects that you view yourself through a harsher filter than others use. People who feel this are often found far more attractive than they believe, tend to be modest and unshowy, and often wave away compliments rather than letting them land.
insight.research: Friends often judge traits like intelligence and creativity more accurately than we judge ourselves.
insight.step: Next compliment you get on how you look, just say 'thank you' and don't argue with it.
